On another more serious note, other people in this thread have been talking Linux gaming. And as the family and friendgroup "techie", I'm thinking about following your lead and starting up a dual boot soon. What distro are you using, and do you like it?

I'm using Linux Mint with the Cinnamon desktop environment at the moment, and I definitely like it. There is a learning curve as to how the Linux system works, but once you get used to it it's quite easy to use. The interface of Mint in particular is very similar to Windows.

Definitely try some Live CDs first. Unlike Windows, in Linux an Install Disc will more often than not boot into a desktop environment which you can test out yourself before deciding to install or not. Most also can automatically detect a preexisting Windows Installation and work around that automatically.

There are some caveats that come with Linux, these are all from my personal experiences. I'm listing these so you and any other Voaters who are interested in Linux don't have to learn them the hard way like I did.

  • Check if your hardware is compatible with Linux before installing. Most is, but my Sound Blaster Z refused to work under Linux, and my RAT 7 caused crashes until I added a custom config file to the system files. Linux Mint has a community run database, which is very useful for checking hardware compatibility.
  • Google is your friend. I'm going to put this in even though I'm assuming most techies already know it, but the solution to most problems can be found by googling a description of the issue. Linux distros are community run, and as such will often have solutions to common problems on their forums.
  • Windows does not like Linux filesystems. There is a free driver out called Ext2Fsd that works pretty well for reading data off of EXT2 and EXT3 partitions, as well as providing write support (which in my experience has only occasionally messed with file permissions, which can be fixed quickly from the file properties dialog box in Mint).
  • Adding to this, DO NOT TRY TO INSTALL WINDOWS GAMES ON AN EXT3 PARTITION, EVEN WITH THE DRIVER ABOVE! I learned this one from experience, annoyance, and Dragon Age not loading properly. That driver can generally handle data, documents and music very well, but executing Windows programs from an EXT3 formatted drive has never worked properly for me.
  • If you decide to uninstall Linux at any point, you will probably also need to reinstall Windows. I'm sure that there's another way to do it, but I haven't needed to uninstall Linux yet, so I wouldn't know about any others.
  • If you want to play modern games (eg. Metro 2033 Redux), use proprietary graphics drivers. The open-source ones don't support the more recent versions of OpenGL, and nVidia's open-source drivers are not great, seeing as they're reverse engineered as opposed to AMD's officially supported open-source drivers.
  • AMD Proprietary Linux drivers are not as good as the Windows drivers at the moment. Nvidia's are, and sometimes even get the edge by a few fps, but with AMD your card will not perform as well as it would on Windows. They're working on this, and with the 300 series they're planning on a complete rewrite, but only time will tell if they're going to fix things.
  • As far as app compatibility goes, out of my 290 Steam games, 121 have native Linux versions, so make of that what you will.
  • You will have to use the terminal at some point. Don't worry, it won't bite. Just know what you're doing beforehand. Most things you can do from a GUI in Linux Mint, but many directions you find will tell you to use the terminal. This is because the terminal works the same across all distros, while the particulars of a distro's UI are different for every distro. Just explore the settings menus and chances are you'll find what you need.

Suffice to say, if you are getting into Linux, be advised it is VERY techie oriented. If at any point you didn't know what I was saying in the above, either stick with Windows and just experiment with VirtualBox (all the fun of Linux without the risk of wrecking your Windows installation, just don't expect good gaming performance), or look around on the web until you know EXACTLY what I've been talking about. Linux is tough to get into, I actually spent a few weeks going over articles related to how I was going to partition my hard drives for it, but if you like messing with computers it's a fun OS to learn.

Keep in mind, this is coming from a dyed in the data techie who's currently trying to run Android in a VM to play apps on my PC, so take any suggestions that something is "easy" with a grain of salt.

[The advice is done, now it's Storytime]

The techie nature of Linux is actually what convinced me to try it out. I was reinstalling Windows because I had gotten a new SSD, and had my saves backed up to an external drive. As it turns out, I forgot to click Safely Remove Hardware, and this actually corrupted my drive. Windows said it needed a reformat, I decided to try a Linux Live CD to see if it would yield better results.

To summarize the Windows error, "Your data's gone, reformat the drive."

To summarize the Linux error, "Something's wrong with your drive, boot to Windows and run [command] to fix some of it and recover what you can."

That command saved my Walking Dead Season 2 save, and that's why I ended up installing Linux.

[End Storytime]
